identity.title: Hypoglycemia history: insulin/sulfonylurea use, missed meals, adrenergic or neuroglycopenic symptoms

technique.how: Ask specifically about insulin or sulfonylurea use (drug, dose, timing of last dose), missed or delayed meals, alcohol, recent renal or hepatic decline, and prodromal autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) or neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, drowsiness, difficulty speaking, weakness). Confirm with a fingerstick glucose at the time of symptoms.
technique.prerequisites: A collateral history when the patient is confused; the medication list including recently added sulfonylureas, insulin dose changes, or drugs that potentiate them.
technique.contraindications: None; the history must never delay a point-of-care glucose in any patient with altered mental status, syncope or focal deficit.

interpretation.positive_finding: Insulin/secretagogue exposure plus a missed meal, alcohol or renal impairment and autonomic or neuroglycopenic prodrome makes hypoglycemia likely; Whipple's triad (symptoms, documented low glucose, resolution with glucose) confirms it.
interpretation.negative_finding: No exposure to insulin or secretagogues and no critical illness, cortisol/hormone deficiency or alcohol makes drug-induced hypoglycemia unlikely, but a measured glucose is still required because neuroglycopenia can present without warning symptoms.
interpretation.pitfalls: Long-standing diabetes and beta-blockers blunt autonomic warning symptoms so neuroglycopenic presentation (confusion, focal deficit) may be the only clue; sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs for 24-72 h so a single corrected glucose is not the end of the episode.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: fingerstick now, treat, and observe for recurrence (sulfonylurea/renal failure -> admit); negative: keep glucose check but move to cardiac/neurologic causes of the spell.

sources.citation: Cryer PE, Axelrod L, Grossman AB, Heller SR, Montori VM, Seaquist ER, Service FJ. Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycemic disorders: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2009;94:709-728.

Hepburn DA, Deary IJ, Frier BM, Patrick AW, Quinn JD, Fisher BM. Symptoms of acute insulin-induced hypoglycemia in humans with and without IDDM. Factor-analysis approach. Diabetes Care 1991;14:949-957.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Never rely on symptom history alone in an obtunded, post-ictal or focally weak patient - measure glucose immediately.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Hypoglycemia with sulfonylurea, insulin overdose, renal failure or alcohol needs monitored admission and repeated glucose; persistent deficit after glucose correction is a stroke workup.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Symptom reporting varies with diabetes duration and awareness status; no interobserver data for the history.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy study (sensitivity/specificity/LR) of hypoglycemia symptom history or insulin/sulfonylurea exposure against a measured-glucose reference standard was found on PubMed (searches: 'hypoglycemia symptoms diabetes sensitivity specificity self-reported'; 'Whipple triad hypoglycemia emergency department symptoms glucose' returned only CGM, paediatric and case-report literature). Evidence is guideline/consensus: Endocrine Society 2009 requires Whipple's triad and names 'Insulin or insulin secretagogue treatment of diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of hypoglycemia' (Abstract). Hepburn 1991 is an experimental symptom-clustering study (autonomic factor: trembling, anxiety, sweating, warmness, nausea; neuroglycopenic factor: dizziness, confusion, tiredness, difficulty speaking, shivering, drowsiness, inability to concentrate; Abstract) with no accuracy data. Prevalence of hypoglycemia among ED syncope/AMS presentations was not extracted.
